questions.text: An attempt row is inserted into login_failures before the password is checked, even for a correct password. Is that right? If so, what does the table hold for a successful login, and when is that row removed?
questions.about: Brute-force limit: Start of an attempt

questions.text: Step 1 already returns 429 when there are 5 or more rows in the last 10 minutes. What does login_lockouts add on top of that? When does a lockout actually change the outcome?
questions.about: Brute-force limit: After a wrong password / login_lockouts

questions.text: If the database fails after the attempt row is committed, for example during the user SELECT or the session insert, what does the user see? Does the failed attempt still count toward the limit?
questions.about: Sequence diagram: opt database error during login

questions.text: Where do users and their password hashes live? Is the users table in the same Postgres, and what does the bcrypt compare run against?
questions.about: Sequence diagram: SELECT user by email

questions.text: How does a browser request reach one of the two instances? Is there a load balancer, and does it matter which instance serves a given request?
When zero rows come back, how does the app find the session row to delete, since the UPDATE matched nothing? And what happens to a user on an expired session who is partway through filling in a form?
The new session is created with expires_at = now + 12h at login. What does the user experience when the 12 hours run out while they are actively using the app?

answers.text: Yes. Every allowed attempt gets a row in the attempts table before bcrypt runs, so parallel guesses all count. For a correct password the row exists only briefly: the login transaction deletes all of that email's attempt and lockout rows. For a wrong password the row stays until the periodic cleanup removes rows older than 10 minutes. I renamed the table from login_failures to login_attempts so the name matches what it holds.

It adds the 15-minute duration. Attempt rows are only counted for 10 minutes, so counting alone would let the email back in about 10 minutes after the 5th failure (or sooner as early rows age out), not 15 minutes. The lockout row is written at the 5th failure with locked_until = now + 15 min. It changes the outcome only in the window after the attempt rows have aged out but before locked_until passes. Requirement 3 demands the 15 minutes.

The user sees the 503 page 'Sign-in is temporarily unavailable'. No session is issued, and if the failure is during the rotation transaction, it rolls back whole, so the old session is untouched. The attempt row was already committed, so yes it still counts. I accept that: it keeps the limit safe, and the cost is that repeated outage errors can briefly lock a real user, which is rare. Recorded in the failure table and open questions.

Yes. The existing users table (id, email lowercase unique, password_hash bcrypt) is in the same Postgres that both instances share, per the brief. The app reads the hash by email and runs the bcrypt comparison in its own process; the database does not do the comparison. Added to the terms.

Yes, a load balancer in front of two identical instances with no sticky sessions, per the brief. It does not matter which instance serves a request, because sessions, attempt counts and the clock all live in the shared Postgres and neither instance keeps state in memory. Added to the overview and terms.

The app already has the hash of the cookie value, so it runs a separate DELETE ... WHERE id_hash = $1; it removes the row if it exists (expired) and does nothing if unknown. For a user mid-form, the next request gets a 303 to /login and their unsent input is lost. After logging in they land on /dashboard, not the page they were on. Returning to the original page is not required by the brief, so I did not add it; listed under open questions.

At 12 hours the session counts as expired, however active the user is. Their next request returns zero rows, the cookie is cleared and they are redirected to /login with no warning, and must sign in again. This follows requirement 6 (12 hours after login, whichever comes first), and expires_at is never extended. A warning or return-to-page flow is not required, so I left it out.

questions.text: POST /logout is a POST that is not /login. Does it go through the session UPDATE check like other protected requests, or does it skip it? What happens if the session is already expired when the user clicks logout?
questions.about: Protected page: any GET or POST except /login / Logout: POST /logout

questions.text: If the separate DELETE after zero rows fails with a database error, what does the user get: the 503 page with the cookie kept, or the redirect to /login with the cookie cleared?

answers.text: POST /logout skips the session UPDATE check. It has its own rule: delete the session row by the cookie's hash if a cookie is present (zero rows is fine), then clear the cookie and 303 to /login. An already-expired session therefore behaves exactly like no session, and the reply is the same. Skipping the check keeps logout identical in every session state, as requirement 8 demands. Clarified in the protected-page section.

The user gets the redirect to /login with the cookie cleared. That delete is best effort: the UPDATE already proved the session is invalid, so no access can be granted, and a 503 would only trap the user on a dead session. The leftover row is removed by the cleanup job. A failure of the UPDATE itself is different and still gives the 503 with the cookie kept.

teachbacks.text:
1. Setup. Two identical app instances sit behind a load balancer that can send any request to either one. Neither keeps state in memory. All state is in the shared Postgres, in `sessions`, `login_attempts` and `login_lockouts`, next to the existing `users` table. The browser holds only a cookie, `__Host-sid`, with a random session ID. The database stores only the SHA-256 hash of that ID.

2. A first visit. The user opens `GET /dashboard` with no cookie. The app sees no cookie and replies 303 to `/login`. This protected-page check applies to every page except `/login` and `/logout`.

3. Login starts. The browser sends `POST /login` with email and password. It may also send an old `sid` cookie. The app trims and lowercases the email and caps it at 254 characters. That normalised email is the key for everything below. Unknown emails are treated exactly like known ones.

4. Reserve the attempt. The app opens a short transaction and takes a Postgres advisory lock on the email, so concurrent attempts for the same email run one at a time. It reads `locked_until` from `login_lockouts` and counts that email's rows in `login_attempts` from the last 10 minutes.
   - If `locked_until` is in the future, or there are 5 or more attempts, it commits without writing. It replies 429 with `Retry-After` and the lockout page. The password is never checked, and retries during a lockout do not extend it.
   - Otherwise it inserts an attempt row and commits. This counts the attempt before the password is checked, so parallel guesses cannot slip past the limit. The lock is released before bcrypt runs because bcrypt is slow.

5. Check the password. The app reads the user by email from `users`. It runs bcrypt in the app, not in the database. If there is no such user, it compares against a fixed dummy hash of the same cost, so timing does not reveal whether the account exists.

6. Wrong password or unknown email. In one transaction under the same advisory lock, the app checks whether there are now 5 or more attempt rows in the last 10 minutes. If so, it upserts `login_lockouts.locked_until = now() + 15 minutes`. It replies 401 with the login page showing "Invalid email or password". No cookie is set or cleared, and any existing session is left alone. The lockout row exists because attempts are counted for only 10 minutes but the lock must last 15.

7. Correct password. In one transaction, the app does the following.
   - It deletes the session that the incoming cookie pointed to, if any.
   - It generates a new random ID (32 bytes from the OS secure random generator, base64url encoded) and inserts a session row. The row holds the hash of the ID, the `user_id`, and `expires_at = now() + 12h`. `created_at` and `last_seen_at` default to `now()`.
   - It deletes all attempt and lockout rows for that email.
   Then it replies 303 to `/dashboard` with `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<new>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/`, with no Max-Age or Expires. The old ID never becomes valid again, which defeats session fixation.

8. A protected request. The browser sends `GET /dashboard` with the cookie, and either instance can receive it. The app hashes the cookie value and runs one atomic statement. It is an `UPDATE sessions SET last_seen_at = now()` that matches `id_hash`, requires `last_seen_at` within the last 30 minutes, requires `expires_at` in the future, and returns `user_id`. It uses the database `now()`, so the instances never compare their own clocks. The same step checks both limits and restarts the idle clock. This happens on every request, with no throttling.
   - One row returned: the session is valid, and the page is served for that user with `Cache-Control: no-store`.
   - Zero rows (unknown or expired): the app tries a best-effort `DELETE` of that session row, and ignores any failure of that delete. It then clears the cookie with `Max-Age=0` and replies 303 to `/login`. Whatever the user was typing is lost. After logging in again they land on `/dashboard`, not the page they were on.
   - The UPDATE itself errors: the app replies with a 503 page, keeps the cookie and does not redirect. This avoids logging users out and avoids redirect loops during a brief outage. Access is never granted on an error.
   - After 12 hours the absolute limit ends the session even for an active user. The next request goes to `/login` with no warning, because the idle clock never extends `expires_at`.

9. Logout. The browser sends `POST /logout`. This path skips the protected-page check. If a cookie is present, the app deletes the session row by hash, and zero rows is fine. It then replies 303 to `/login` and clears the cookie, with the same reply whether or not a session existed. If the delete errors, it replies 503 "We couldn't sign you out. Please try again." and keeps the cookie so the user can retry.

10. Background cleanup. Each instance runs a job every 5 minutes, guarded by `pg_try_advisory_lock` so only one runs at a time.
   - It deletes sessions that are idle for more than 30 minutes or past `expires_at`.
   - It deletes attempt rows older than 10 minutes.
   - It deletes lockouts whose `locked_until` has passed.
   This only limits table size. Security does not depend on it. If the job fails, it logs and retries on the next tick.

11. Login failures. A database error before the attempt is recorded gives a 503 "Sign-in is temporarily unavailable", with no password check and no session. An error after the attempt is recorded (user lookup or session insert) gives the same 503. The attempt row is already committed and still counts toward the limit. The session transaction rolls back whole, so the old session stays and no new one exists. Repeated outage errors can lock a real user out for up to 15 minutes, which the document accepts. A 6th concurrent request can get a 429 even if the 5th attempt turns out correct. Per-IP limits and login CSRF protection are out of scope.
gaps: The document does not say how the app tells whether a request is for a protected page versus `/login` or `/logout`, such as middleware or routing. It also does not say what the app does with the returned `user_id` beyond 'serve the page for that user'.

It does not say where the Retry-After value comes from, for example whether it is derived from `locked_until` or from the 10-minute window, when 429 is returned because of 5 or more attempts with no lockout row yet.
It does not say what a GET /login request does (rendering the login form), or what an already signed-in user who visits /login sees. It only describes POST /login.
It does not say what the app does if the incoming `sid` cookie at login is malformed or invalid, beyond 'delete the session it pointed to, if any'.
It does not say what the cleanup job's schedule or lock key looks like per instance, or how the 5-minute timer is started inside the app.
